title: Non-planar contact structures with Calabi-Yau Fillings and topological quantum computation
abstract: This paper is a non-planar counterpart of the author's earlier work on planar contact structures and topological quantum computation. There the page is planar and all branch points are paired by disjoint liftable arcs, compatibly with the joint eigenlines of the Ising representation and with Calabi-Yau (CY) Stein fillings, those with vanishing first Chern class. Here the page has genus g and connected binding, presented as a simple degree-three cover of the disk. Every maximal system of disjoint liftable arcs has exactly g members and leaves two branch points unused. The half-twist interchanging the two points is not liftable, but its cube is, and lifts to the identity. An integral residue criterion supplies the CY test. A factorization localized on a contact connected sum is automatically CY. Unlike in the planar case, a CY factorization need not be the shortest. Once the fusion channels of the g pairs are fixed, Ising fusion determines the channel of the remaining pair, and braiding acts there only by scalars. Fibonacci fusion can leave that channel undetermined, and the powers of the cube then act by ten distinct relative phases on a single joint eigenspace, while the CY Stein filling stays fixed
summary: This work generalizes topological quantum computation theory to non-planar settings by analyzing contact structures with Calabi-Yau fillings. It establishes that the CY condition imposes constraints on the underlying geometry, and crucially, it distinguishes between Ising and Fibonacci anyon models based on whether the quantum state retains a relative phase after fixing the geometric structure.
main_problem: The paper extends the study of topological quantum computation from planar to non-planar contact structures, linking geometric properties (Calabi-Yau fillings) to quantum field theories (Ising and Fibonacci anyons).
main_result: In the non-planar case, the CY condition is not restricted to the shortest factorization, and the choice between Ising and Fibonacci fusion rules dictates whether a relative phase can remain undetermined on the resulting quantum state.
method: The analysis combines algebraic topology (Riemann-Hurwitz formula, homology, vanishing cycles) with concepts from quantum field theory (fusion rules, braid representations) to derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the Calabi-Yau property.
model_or_system: The system involves a surface $P$ of genus $g$ with a connected binding, which is modeled as a degree-three cover of the disk. The quantum side is governed by anyonic models, specifically Ising and Fibonacci theories, whose fusion channels determine the structure of the quantum state.
key_observables: Calabi-Yau (CY) condition ($c_1(W)=0$), dimension of joint eigenspaces, relative phases, and the structure of the maximal system of disjoint liftable arcs.
important_parameters: Genus $g$, number of branch points $n=2g+2$, and the specific fusion rules of the underlying anyon models.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the binding is connected and relies on the existence of a Hurwitz system for the branch set $\Delta$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the non-planar topological framework (genus $g$ cover), then deriving the integral residue criterion for the CY condition, and finally comparing the implications of the CY condition on the quantum structure using Ising versus Fibonacci fusion rules.
why_interesting: It provides a deep mathematical framework connecting geometric invariants (CY manifolds) to the algebraic constraints imposed by different topological quantum field theories (Ising/Fibonacci), which is central to understanding fault-tolerant quantum computation.
